items.explanation: The historian's contrast needs qualifying on both sides. Massachusetts Bay limited voting to male church members, excluding most adult men, while Virginia had an elected assembly from 1619 -- so neither region was democratic by modern standards, and the gap between them was narrower than the claim suggests.
items.fact_source: House of Burgesses convened at Jamestown, 1619 -- first elected legislative assembly in the colonies; Massachusetts Bay restricted voting to male church members (1631).

option_explanations.A: Wrong. This jumps a century from town meetings to the Revolution, assuming the earlier practice directly caused the later outcome -- and it makes one practice the whole explanation of colonial political development.
option_explanations.B: Right. It brings specific counter-evidence from both sides -- a restricted franchise in New England and an early elected assembly in Virginia -- that narrows the claimed gap.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. It reduces a political difference to one economic cause, leaving no room for the elected assembly Virginia actually had or the restricted franchise New England actually had.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. It treats the existence of an elected assembly as proof of broad popular control, ignoring property limits on voting and the planter elite's dominance of Virginia politics.

options: (A) New England's town meetings directly caused the region's later leadership in the independence movement, which shows that local self-government was the decisive force in colonial political development.
(B) Voting in Massachusetts Bay was limited to male church members, excluding most adult men, while Virginia elected representatives to the House of Burgesses as early as 1619.
(C) Because the Chesapeake's plantation economy differed from New England's mixed economy, economic differences alone explain why the two regions developed different political systems.
(D) Because Virginians elected members of the House of Burgesses, ordinary Virginians controlled their government as fully as New Englanders controlled theirs through town meetings.
items.stem: Which of the following most weakens the historian's comparison?

stimulus.text: A historian argues: 'New England's town meetings created a more democratic political culture than the Chesapeake's, where a small planter elite monopolized political power.'

items.explanation: The statutes on paper restricted colonial trade, but paper and practice differed: enforcement was loose during the era of salutary neglect, smuggling was widespread, and the empire gave colonists naval protection and favored access to English markets. The burden was real but smaller than the laws suggest -- and reading the law's purpose or its date as proof of its effects confuses intent and sequence with outcomes.
items.fact_source: Navigation Acts (1651, 1660, 1663): enumerated goods; lax enforcement during salutary neglect; widespread smuggling; colonies benefited from Royal Navy protection and access to English markets.

option_explanations.A: Right. It weighs the laws against how they were actually enforced and what colonists received in return, showing the 'impoverished' claim is overstated.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. That Parliament wrote the laws to favor England describes their purpose, not their effect -- a law's intent does not prove how much poorer anyone became.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. New England's growth does not show the laws cost nobody anything; one region's success cannot stand in for all the colonies.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. That the Revolution came later does not prove the acts' economic damage caused it -- sequence is not causation, and the Revolution grew from later taxes and political conflicts.

options: (A) Enforcement was loose during the era of salutary neglect, smuggling was widespread, and the colonies received naval protection and favored access to English markets.
(B) Parliament wrote the laws to enrich England at the colonies' expense, and that purpose alone proves the laws made the colonies poorer than they would otherwise have been.
(C) New England's trade-based economy kept growing under the acts, which shows the laws imposed no real costs on colonial trade anywhere.
(D) The acts restricted colonial trade in the 1600s and the Revolution followed in the 1770s, so the economic damage they caused drove the colonies to independence.
items.stem: Which of the following best evaluates this argument?

stimulus.text: A historian argues: 'British mercantilist laws, especially the Navigation Acts, impoverished the North American colonies by choking off their trade with the wider world.'

items.explanation: Smith's purpose limits what his account can prove. He was writing to win English support for the colony, which gave him reason to tell a dramatic story, and the episode may have been a ritual ceremony whose meaning he misunderstood. Because of those limits, the account cannot settle what Pocahontas herself intended.
items.fact_source: Smith described his December 1607 capture by the Powhatan and Pocahontas's intervention in a 1616 letter to Queen Anne and in his 1624 General Historie of Virginia, a promotional history aimed at English readers; historians have suggested the scene was an adoption or initiation ritual. Pocahontas was baptized as Rebecca and married the colonist John Rolfe in 1614.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. It treats an eyewitness account as automatically true and assumes later evidence could never challenge it -- being the earliest surviving account does not make an account reliable.
option_explanations.B: Right. It names two specific limits on the source -- Smith's promotional purpose and the chance that he misunderstood a ritual -- and draws the correct conclusion about what the account cannot prove.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. It takes a real limit of one source and stretches it into a rule against every English account of the period -- judging a whole category of sources from a single case.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. It reads later events -- baptism and marriage -- backward as proof of what Pocahontas intended years earlier, assuming that what happened later reveals her earlier motives.

options: (A) Smith was the only English witness to the event, and his published account is the earliest surviving record of it, so his version cannot be challenged by later evidence.
(B) Smith wrote years later to win English support for the colony, and the 'rescue' may have been a ritual whose meaning he misunderstood, so the account cannot establish her motives.
(C) Because England competed with Spain for empire, all English colonial writings of this period were propaganda and cannot be used as evidence about Native peoples.
(D) Pocahontas later accepted baptism and married the English colonist John Rolfe in 1614, which confirms that she had already sympathized with the English and opposed her father's decision.
items.stem: A student claims that Smith's account proves Pocahontas personally opposed her father's decision and saved Smith's life. Which of the following best evaluates that claim?

stimulus.text: English colonist John Smith's 1624 General Historie describes his 1607 capture by the Powhatan: he wrote that Chief Powhatan ordered his execution, and that the chief's daughter Pocahontas threw herself over him and saved his life. The account appeared years after the event, in a book Smith wrote to promote Virginia to English readers.

items.explanation: The claim treats the slave system as finished in 1619, but Virginia built the legal machinery of racial slavery decades later -- making bondage hereditary through the mother and closing the baptism path to freedom. That legal development was a real change, not a continuation of 1619, so the mid-1700s system was not the one that began in 1619.
items.fact_source: First Africans arrived in Virginia in 1619 ('20 and odd Negroes'); Virginia's 1662 statute made enslaved status hereditary through the mother (partus sequitur ventrem); a 1667 statute held that baptism did not free an enslaved person; a comprehensive slave code followed in 1705.

option_explanations.A: Right. It gives specific evidence of change after 1619 -- new laws that created hereditary, race-based bondage -- which directly contradicts the claim that the system was established in 1619 and stayed the same.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. It assumes that because enslaved Africans were present in 1619, a complete slave system existed immediately -- confusing the arrival of enslaved people with the creation of the legal institution of slavery.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. It makes one cause -- tobacco profits -- the whole explanation, leaving no room for the laws that actually created hereditary racial slavery; a single cause cannot carry the whole story.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. It assumes every colony's slave system worked identically because both were English -- overgeneralizing from one colony's laws to all of them.

options: (A) In the 1660s Virginia passed laws making enslaved status pass from mother to child and denying freedom to the baptized, showing the system took shape decades after 1619.
(B) Because English planters wanted African labor from the start, the change from indentured servants to enslaved Africans in the Chesapeake was complete within a year of the 1619 arrival.
(C) The profitable tobacco economy was the single cause of slavery's growth, so Virginia's slave system would have looked the same in 1754 even without the laws passed in the 1660s.
(D) Africans in Virginia were enslaved on exactly the same legal terms and faced identical legal conditions as Africans in Barbados, since both colonies lived under the same English law.
items.stem: Which of the following most weakens the historian's claim?

stimulus.text: A historian argues: 'The arrival of enslaved Africans in Virginia in 1619 established race-based slavery in the British colonies, and the plantation slavery of the mid-1700s was essentially the same system that began in 1619.'
